DAMA-DMBOK2 Data Management Body of Knowledge (2nd edition (2017))
One assessment, three vocabularies. These are not three independent measurements — they are one evidence base expressed in three
published frameworks. The three overall figures landing close together is the CORRECT result: the same answers, projected through the same
35 TACR sections. What differs between them is emphasis and structure, which is what makes each one legible to a different audience.
RETAINED SHARE is how much of the framework’s own definition of a dimension is in scope for this assessment. SCORED SHARE is how
much of what is in scope was actually measured. They answer different questions and are never combined: a dimension can be fully retained
and barely scored, or the reverse, and a single "coverage" number would hide whichever is worse.
RETAINED SHARE here is structural, not scope-driven. This assessment has no core/banking split, so a leaf dimension is either fully mapped
(100% retained) or mapped by nothing at all (0%, and reported as NOT APPLICABLE rather than scored). A framework’s own retained share
falls below 100% precisely when one of its leaves is unreachable from this assessment. Where the two shares diverge on a leaf, the cause is
always what has been ANSWERED, never what is in scope.
A dimension is SCORED, NOT ASSESSED or NOT APPLICABLE, and the last two never render as 0. "Not assessed" means the framework
defines it, it is in scope, and nobody has answered the questions behind it yet. "Not applicable" means this assessment asks nothing that could
evidence it. A zero would read as "measured, and bad" for both.
All figures are on the TAIW 1-5 maturity scale. They are NOT rescaled to each framework’s own scale — DCAM scores 1-6 and COBIT 2019
uses capability levels 0-5. A DCAM component shown here as 3.2 is 3.2 out of 5, not out of 6.
What is published and what is ours
Framework names, codes and dimension structures are PUBLISHED content. The relative WEIGHTS applied to those
dimensions are Godaitec editorial judgement — none of these frameworks publishes weightings for its own dimensions. The
weights are the first thing to challenge in review, and changing them changes every figure derived from them.
DMBOK2 (2nd edition (2017)) — Published structure, high confidence.
What TAIW's assessment can and cannot evidence
DGI IS NOT OFFERED. DGI reaches 59% of itself on TACR. Decision Rights, Accountabilities, the Data Governance Office and Data
Stewards are mapped by nothing, because a customs assessment does not ask who chairs a data governance council. A DGI score built on
the 59% that does map would carry an invisible 41% gap, so DGI is not offered at all. The four dimensions it loses are Decision Rights,
Accountabilities, Data Governance Office, Data Stewards — which is close to a definition of what DGI is. This is a finding about TACR, not a
defect in DGI: the same ten DGI leaves reach 100% of themselves on HAIW's HACR subcategories.
DM07 IS NOT APPLICABLE. Document & Content Management. 0 of 640 TACR questions mention document or content management.
Customs runs on declarations, manifests and certificates, so this is a real gap in the ASSESSMENT rather than an absence in the domain —
and forcing it onto Clearance Automation would be a mapping nobody could defend. HAIW does not share it: DM07 lands on
ii_document_exchange there, because health runs on clinical documents.
THREE FRAMEWORKS, NOT FOUR. Every figure on this document is a projection of ONE TACR assessment onto DMBOK2, DCAM and
COBIT 2019. Nothing here is a second opinion; the frameworks cannot corroborate one another because they are reading the same

Retained and scored share are SEPARATE columns on purpose. Retained is how much of the framework’s own definition this assessment
covers; scored is how much of that was measured. Combining them would hide whichever is worse.
None. Every leaf dimension of DMBOK2 is either mapped in full or mapped by nothing — there is no scope filter on this
assessment that could retain part of one. DMBOK2's own retained share of 94% above is the weighted mean over its 11 leaves,
and it falls below 100% exactly when one of them is unreachable, which is listed under "Not applicable" below.

Why each dimension maps to the TACR sections it does
Every row below was authored deliberately. A mapping a consultant cannot defend in a room is not a mapping, and this section is the room.
The one TACR question that names data governance mechanics directly — "master data
governance clearly define ownership, stewardship, and approval workflows" — sits here. It is the
closest TACR comes to DMBOK's decision-rights core.
Data-sharing MOUs that define scope, formats and update frequencies are governance
instruments: they are where TACR asks whether the administration has agreed rules with other
A documented data protection and privacy policy governing all customs data is a governance
artefact, and TACR measures whether one exists and is enforced.
The warehouse section asks whether an analytics data platform exists and integrates WeBOC,
PSW and partner sources — the enterprise data architecture question, in TACR's vocabulary.
The digital vision section carries the only architecture-principle question in TACR: whether the
technology strategy mandates API-first architecture for all customs integrations.
PSW is the national integration architecture; how much of the regulatory estate it covers is an
architectural fact, not just an operational one.
The WCO Data Model IS a published data model, and this section asks whether Pakistan Customs
has mapped its elements to WCO DM 3.x information packages and built message implementation
profiles. That is data modelling and design, done against a standard.
Warehouse design — how source systems are integrated into an analytical model — is the other
place TACR asks a modelling question.
Data centre capacity, storage adequacy for growing customs data volumes and long-term retention
are storage and operations in the DMBOK sense.
Workload placement across public, private and hybrid environments, and data-residency
compliance, is where storage decisions are actually made.
Role-based access control on a need-to-know basis and complete audit trails for access,
modification and deletion are the data-security controls DMBOK names.
The cybersecurity strategy, endpoint protection and intrusion detection are the infrastructure half of
PSW is the integration hub: how many OGAs are electronically integrated is the headline
Whether OGAs return clearance decisions through standardised APIs, in real time, is
interoperability measured at the interface rather than at the platform.
WeBOC is the transactional system every integration terminates in; its coverage and data
completeness bound what any integration can carry.
A one-to-one match. This section asks about authoritative master data for traders and brokers, tariff
codes managed as reference data with change history, and harmonised port/country/currency
codes. That is the whole of DMBOK's Reference & Master Data.
The warehouse itself: whether one exists, what it integrates, and whether ETL/ELT pipelines are
The BI half: standardised dashboards for management, self-service reporting by trained officers,
revenue drill-down. DMBOK treats warehousing and BI as one knowledge area and TACR splits
them, so both halves are named.

Mapping data elements to the WCO Data Model and maintaining message implementation profiles
is the nearest thing TACR has to a managed metadata registry: it is where element definitions live
The warehouse section carries TACR's only business-glossary and catalogue questions. THIS IS A
THIN MAPPING and the retained share does not say so: TACR asks two metadata questions in
640. Read the dimension score with that in mind.
A one-to-one match. Rules defined for critical data elements, automated validation at point of entry
in WeBOC and PSW, and metrics monitored against thresholds — DMBOK's Data Quality, in full.

What this assessment does not cover
These dimensions are mapped by nothing: this assessment asks no question that could evidence them. They are not failures
and they are NOT scored as zero — the framework defines something the assessment does not reach.
Dimensions scored from part of their evidence
None. Every dimension that is scored at all is scored from every TACR section mapped to it.
7 of 35 TACR sections are reached by none of the 3 frameworks. They are still SCORED on the assessment and they still
appear in TAIW's own maturity report — they simply contribute to no framework scorecard, because no published
These are customs operations rather than data management: TFA commitments, clearance and revenue automation, risk models, compliance
rates and officer training. No published data-management framework defines them, and mapping them onto one anyway would be a mapping
nobody could defend in a room. They are measured, they carry a maturity score, and they appear in the TAIW maturity report — they are simply
outside what DMBOK2, DCAM and COBIT 2019 are about. WTO TFA Commitment is the clearest case: it is eighteen questions, one per TFA
Article, so the framework’s vocabulary IS the assessment and a projection would restate it against itself.
DCAM is modelled at v2.2. Its capability and sub-capability levels beneath each component are deliberately NOT authored: they were not
recalled reliably enough to put in front of an auditor, and an absent level is recoverable where an invented one is not. DCAM v3.0
reorganised the model and is not what is represented here.
COBIT 2019 APO14 sub-practice titles have been checked against a public COBIT 2019 reference and corrected where they differed. They
have NOT been checked against the ISACA publication itself, which is the only source an audit function should accept — treat them as
verified secondhand, not as quoted. The five EDM governance objectives are high confidence.
